planting.note: Basal offsets can be separated once they have their own root mass, but leaving the clump intact produces a fuller multi-stem specimen faster.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil enriched with compost and water regularly until new offsets establish their own roots. Unlike typical single-trunked windmill palms, this variety produces basal suckers that form a multi-stemmed clump over time, so allow extra lateral space. Remove only dead or damaged fronds, since the palm relies on a full canopy for energy during cool winters. Mulch the root zone in colder zones to protect the shallow-rooted offsets through hard freezes.
sources: Riffle & Craft, An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms

common_name: Bonin Island Fan Palm (Dwarf Chinese Fan Palm)

planting.note: This variety stays more compact than typical Livistona chinensis, making it a better fit for smaller Gulf Coast landscapes.

directions: Set out in rich, well-drained soil and irrigate consistently through the first two summers to build a deep root system. This Bonin Island native variety grows more slowly and stays noticeably smaller and more cold-tolerant than the typical form of the species, with rounder fruit and a denser crown. Give it a sheltered spot for the first few winters in the cooler end of its range, since young plants are more frost-sensitive than established specimens. Once trunking, it tolerates brief dips into the low 20s Fahrenheit with only minor foliar burn.
sources: Riffle & Craft, An Encyclopedia of Cultivated Palms
